chapter.name: Linear Programming
chapter.blurb: A linear programming problem seeks the maximum or minimum value of a linear objective function of non-negative variables subject to a set of linear constraints. The chapter formulates such a problem mathematically from a real-life situation and solves two-variable problems by the graphical Corner Point Method, covering bounded and unbounded feasible regions, multiple optimal solutions and problems with no feasible region.

scope_in.item: Recognise an optimisation problem and a linear programming problem as a special type of it, and say what 'linear' and 'programming' mean
Identify the objective function Z = ax + by, the decision variables, the constraints and the non-negative restrictions of a given linear programming problem, and evaluate Z at a given point

Formulate a simple two-variable real-life problem of the furniture-dealer kind (limited money, limited storage or time, profit per item) as a linear programming problem: variables, linear constraints, non-negativity and objective function
Define and identify the feasible region, infeasible region, feasible solution, infeasible solution and optimal solution; test whether a given point is feasible
Say whether a feasible region is bounded or unbounded (can or cannot be enclosed within a circle), know that it is always convex, and find its corner points as intersections of boundary lines
State and use Theorems 1 and 2 (without proof): an optimal value occurs at a corner point; on a bounded region both a maximum and a minimum exist at corner points
Apply the Corner Point Method to a bounded feasible region: evaluate Z at every corner point and pick the largest and smallest values
Recognise multiple optimal solutions: when two corner points give the same optimal value, every point on the segment joining them does

For an unbounded feasible region, decide whether the largest or smallest corner value M or m is the maximum or minimum by testing the open half plane ax + by > M or ax + by < m against the feasible region
Recognise a problem whose constraints have no common point as having no feasible region and hence no feasible solution

concepts.name: Linear programming problem and its terms
concepts.description: Recognising a linear programming problem as a special optimisation problem and naming its objective function, decision variables, constraints and non-negative restrictions.
concepts.idea: A linear programming problem asks for the largest or smallest value of a linear function of non-negative variables that must also satisfy some linear inequalities.
concepts.rule: Objective function Z = ax + by is what is maximised or minimised; x and y are the decision variables; the linear inequalities, including x >= 0 and y >= 0, are the constraints. Everything must be linear.
concepts.example: Maximise Z = 250x + 75y subject to 5x + y <= 100, x + y <= 60, x >= 0, y >= 0: Z is the objective function, x and y the decision variables, and the four inequalities are the constraints.

questions.a: (P) The objective function and both constraints are linear, but the definition also requires the variables to be non-negative; the restrictions x >= 0, y >= 0 are missing, so as stated it does not meet the definition until they are added. (Q) The constraints are linear and the variables are non-negative, but Z = xy is not a linear function of x and y, so (Q) is not a linear programming problem.

questions.q: Riya says: 'An optimisation problem and a linear programming problem mean exactly the same thing.' Is she right? Justify from the textbook's description of the two terms.
questions.a: She is not right. Optimisation problems are the general class of problems that seek to maximise or minimise a quantity such as profit or cost. Linear programming problems are a special but very important type of optimisation problem, in which a linear objective function is optimised subject to linear constraints with non-negative variables.
s: States that linear programming problems are a special type of optimisation problem, not the same thing
Gives what makes it linear programming: linear objective function, linear constraints, non-negative variables

s: Linear objective function Z = ax + by to be maximised
Exactly two linear constraints plus x >= 0, y >= 0
Correctly names the objective function, decision variables and constraints

concepts.name: Mathematical formulation of a linear programming problem
concepts.description: Turning a two-variable real-life situation into variables, linear constraints, non-negative restrictions and a linear objective function.
concepts.idea: Each limited resource in the story becomes one inequality and the quantity to be made largest or smallest becomes the objective function.
concepts.rule: Choose x and y as the quantities to decide; write 'at most' as <= and 'at least' as >=; add x >= 0, y >= 0; write profit or cost as Z = ax + by.
concepts.example: Tables cost Rs 2500, chairs Rs 500, Rs 50,000 available, at most 60 pieces: 5x + y <= 100, x + y <= 60, x >= 0, y >= 0; profit Z = 250x + 75y.

concepts.name: Feasible region and feasible solutions
concepts.description: The feasible region as the common region of all constraints, feasible, infeasible and optimal solutions, bounded and unbounded regions, and corner points.
concepts.idea: The feasible region is the set of all points that satisfy every constraint at once; each of its points is a possible choice.
concepts.rule: A point is feasible only if it satisfies all constraints, including x >= 0, y >= 0. The region is bounded if it can be enclosed within a circle. A corner point is the intersection of two boundary lines lying in the region.
concepts.example: For 5x + y <= 100, x + y <= 60, x >= 0, y >= 0 the feasible region has corner points (0, 0), (20, 0), (10, 50), (0, 60); (10, 50) is feasible and (25, 40) is infeasible.

concepts.name: Unbounded feasible regions and problems with no solution
concepts.description: Deciding by the open half plane test whether a corner value is really the maximum or minimum on an unbounded feasible region, and recognising problems with no feasible region.
concepts.idea: On an unbounded region the corner values are only candidates: Z may keep growing or falling without limit, so the candidate must be tested.
concepts.rule: M is the maximum only if ax + by > M has no point in common with the feasible region; m is the minimum only if ax + by < m has none. If no point satisfies all constraints there is no feasible region and no solution.
concepts.example: Z = -50x + 20y on the unbounded region with corners (0, 5), (0, 3), (1, 0), (6, 0): smallest corner value -300, but -50x + 20y < -300 meets the region, so Z has no minimum.
